section.title: Problem
section.p: When an agent response contains N tool calls, `Froth.Agent.Worker` does the obvious thing: it spawns N concurrent Tasks.
The concurrency stops there.
Each Task immediately calls the same GenServer:
In the Telegram bots, `tool_executor` is the bot process. That process handles:
which means all tool executions are serialized through one mailbox.
So the current shape is:
section.code: worker spawns N Tasks -> all N Tasks queue on one GenServer.call -> bot executes tool 1 -> tool 2 waits -> tool 3 waits -> ...
section.p: The result is the worst of both worlds:

item.p: the worker thinks it is doing parallel tool execution
the bot process is actually doing serialized tool execution
the queue is governed by the OTP default `GenServer.call` timeout of 5000ms

section.p: If tool call #1 takes long enough, tool call #2 can fail before it ever starts running.

section.title: Why This Is Happening
section.p: The serialization is not intentional. It is a consequence of the bot process wearing two hats:

item.p: it is the Telegram event router and state owner
it is also the tool executor

section.p: Some of that state is genuinely needed by tools:
But needing state access is not the same as needing serialized execution.
The code path today mixes three different responsibilities inside one GenServer call:

item.p: perform the actual tool work and network I/O
mutate bot state based on the result

section.p: That is the real bug.

section.title: A Second Bug Hidden Inside the First One
section.p: The current draft of this RFC could tempt a one-line fix:
That does remove the accidental 5000ms timeout. But in the current code there is no separate worker-owned timeout for tool tasks.
So today:
Both are wrong.
Timeout policy should belong to `Froth.Agent.Worker`, because the worker owns the lifecycle of the tool tasks.

section.title: Requirements
section.p: Any real fix should satisfy all of these:

item.p: Tool work should run in parallel when the tools are independent.
Bot state must remain internally consistent.
External side effects should not require the bot GenServer to sit blocked on network I/O.
Timeouts must be explicit and owned by the worker, not inherited from `GenServer.call`.
The model should compose with RFC-0004's execution-log and telemetry direction.

subsection.title: 1. Move timeout ownership into `Agent.Worker`
subsection.p: Add a `tool_timeout_ms` config value and have the worker schedule a timeout per invocation. If a tool exceeds its deadline:

item.p: the worker records a failed tool result
the cycle continues or fails according to policy

subsection.p: Only after this exists should the internal `GenServer.call` timeout be set to `:infinity`, because at that point the worker is the owner of the deadline.

subsection.title: 2. Split tool execution into `prepare`, `execute`, and `commit`
subsection.p: The core change is to separate state access from work.
The bot process handles a fast call that:

item.p: reserves any state that must be claimed atomically

subsection.p: This step should not perform network I/O or long-running work.

item.p: whether a control prompt should be shown

subsection.p: The worker Task executes the tool outside the bot GenServer using the prepared capsule.
Execution returns both a result and a list of state effects.
After execution completes, the bot process handles a fast commit step that applies the serialized state mutations:

item.p: any bookkeeping around cycle prompts and task tracking

subsection.p: This preserves state consistency without forcing the actual work through one mailbox.

section.title: Why This Fits the Current Code
section.p: The existing bot code already reveals the correct split.
`execute_tool_call/3` currently mixes together:
Those should become separate phases instead of one blocking call.
Even the special cases point in the same direction:

item.p: `send_message` does network I/O plus sent-message bookkeeping
`run_shell` and `elixir_eval` need control-prompt reservation and optional narration, but not a blocked bot mailbox
`maybe_inject_mid_cycle_messages/2` is a commit concern, not an execution concern

subsection.title: Not just "increase the timeout"
subsection.p: Changing `5000` to `30000` reduces pain but keeps the architecture wrong. It preserves serialization and leaves the timeout policy in the wrong layer.

subsection.title: Not just `:infinity` without worker deadlines
subsection.p: That only swaps one accidental policy for another.

subsection.title: Not a process pool first
subsection.p: A pool of tool executors may make sense later, but it does not solve the fact that execution, state access, and commit are currently collapsed into one operation. Fix the boundary first.

section.p: Phase 1: Add explicit `tool_timeout_ms` to `Agent.Config` and make
Phase 2: Set internal `GenServer.call` timeouts for tool execution
section.code: to `:infinity`, now that the worker owns the deadline.
section.p: Phase 3: Replace `{:execute, tool_use, context}` with a `prepare`
section.code: step that returns a lightweight execution capsule.
section.p: Phase 4: Execute tools in Tasks outside the bot GenServer and return
Phase 5: Add a `commit` step in the bot process for serialized state
Phase 6: Emit `tool.started`, `tool.completed`, `tool.failed`, and
section.code: `tool.timed_out` events in a form that can attach cleanly to RFC-0004's execution spine.

item.p: Parallel tool execution becomes real, not performative.
Tool timeouts become explicit and debuggable.
Bot state remains consistent without forcing network I/O through one mailbox.
The execution model becomes a better fit for persistence and telemetry.
More moving parts in the tool-execution path.
A new prepared execution capsule / commit-effects abstraction.
Some tool behavior currently expressed as direct state mutation will need to be refactored.

section.title: Recommendation
section.p: Do this in two deliberate steps:

item.p: move timeout ownership into the worker immediately
then split tool execution into `prepare`, `execute`, and `commit`

section.p: That fixes the current failure mode without pretending the real issue was just a magic number.
